ing: fermented durian; or use extra lime juice and a little mashed ripe mango
st: Heat [[1 tbsp]] oil in a skillet over medium heat and fry the shallots and garlic for 2 minutes until soft.
Add the fish and cook 3 minutes per side until it flakes easily, then break it into chunks with a spoon.
Stir in the tempoyak, chilies and the juice of [[1 lime]], cook 2 minutes, and season with salt. Set this dip aside.
In a heatproof bowl, whisk [[1 cup]] sago starch with [[1 cup]] cold water until smooth and milky.
Pour in [[2 cups]] freshly boiled water all at once, stirring hard with a wooden spoon or chopsticks.
Keep stirring for 1 to 2 minutes as the mixture turns thick, glossy and translucent like glue.
Twist a portion of the sticky ambuyat around chopsticks or a fork and drag it through the sour dip.
Squeeze the juice of the remaining [[1 lime]] over the dip and serve at once, since ambuyat stiffens as it cools.
Rinse [[2 cups]] rice in cold water until it runs mostly clear, then drain it.
Cook the rice with [[2.5 cups]] water and [[0.5 tsp]] salt, covered, over low heat for 15 minutes. Rest 10 minutes off the heat.
Mix the garlic, ginger, turmeric and [[1.5 tsp]] salt into a paste and rub it over the chicken.
Let the chicken marinate in the fridge for at least 20 minutes.
Dust the chicken with [[3 tbsp]] cornstarch and shake off the extra.
Heat [[2 cups]] oil in a heavy pot to 340°F (170°C). Fry the chicken in batches for 12 to 15 minutes, turning often, until golden and the center reaches 165°F (74°C).
Drain the chicken on paper towels.
Pile rice on each plate and top with a piece of fried chicken, a big spoonful of sambal and sliced cucumber.
Drain the soaked chilies and blend them with the ginger, galangal, garlic and shallots into a smooth paste, adding a splash of water if needed.
Add the paste, coconut milk, lemongrass, lime leaves, turmeric and [[2 tsp]] salt to a wide heavy pot with the beef.
Bring to a boil over medium-high heat, stirring often, then lower to a gentle simmer.
Simmer uncovered for 1.5 hours, stirring every 10 minutes so nothing sticks, until the sauce is thick and the beef is nearly tender.
Stir in [[1 tbsp]] brown sugar and the toasted coconut.
Keep cooking 45 to 60 minutes on low heat, stirring more often, until the oil separates and the sauce clings to the beef as a dark, dry coating.
Remove the lemongrass and lime leaves, taste, and add salt if needed.
Rest 10 minutes and serve with steamed rice.
Rinse [[2 cups]] rice until the water runs clear and drain well.
Combine the rice, [[1.5 cups]] coconut milk, [[1 cup]] water, pandan leaves and [[1 tsp]] salt in a pot.
Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes. Rest, covered, for 10 minutes.
Boil the eggs in water for 10 minutes, then cool in cold water and peel.
Heat [[0.5 cup]] oil in a small pan over medium heat. Fry the peanuts 2 to 3 minutes until golden, then lift out with a slotted spoon.
Fry the anchovies in the same oil for 2 minutes until crisp and drain on paper towels.
Fluff the rice with a fork and remove the pandan leaves.
Serve rice with sambal, peanuts, anchovies, halved eggs and cucumber slices.

ing: about 8x10 inches each; or use parchment and foil
for soaking, plus more for steaming
st: Rinse [[2 cups]] glutinous rice and soak it in cold water for 4 hours or overnight, then drain well.
Mix the rice with [[1.5 cups]] coconut milk and [[1 tsp]] salt.
Soften the banana leaves by passing them over a low flame or dipping in hot water for 30 seconds, then wipe dry.
Place a leaf flat and spoon about [[0.25 cup]] of rice into a log at one end.
Roll the leaf around the rice into a tight cylinder and fold in the ends, tucking them under. Tie with kitchen string if needed.
Set a steamer over boiling water with the pandan leaves in the water, then arrange the bundles on the rack.
Steam covered for 60 minutes, topping up the water when needed, until the rice is soft and sticky.
Cool for 10 minutes, then unwrap and serve with curry or as a side.
Blend the lemongrass, shallots, garlic, turmeric, [[1 tbsp]] sugar and [[1 tsp]] salt into a rough paste.
Toss the chicken with the paste and [[0.25 cup]] coconut milk, then marinate in the fridge for at least 30 minutes.
Thread the chicken onto soaked skewers, three or four pieces each.
For the sauce, grind the peanuts, chilies, [[1 tbsp]] sugar and [[0.5 tsp]] salt in a blender until crumbly.
Fry the mixture in [[1 tbsp]] oil for 3 minutes, then add [[0.5 cup]] water, [[0.25 cup]] coconut milk and the tamarind. Simmer 8 minutes until thick.
Heat a grill or grill pan to medium-high and brush with [[1 tbsp]] oil.
Grill the skewers 3 to 4 minutes per side until charred in spots and cooked to 165°F (74°C).
Serve the satay hot with the warm peanut sauce.
Wrap [[1 tbsp]] shrimp paste in foil and press flat.
Toast the packet in a dry skillet over medium heat for 2 minutes per side. Open a window, because it smells strong.
Roughly chop the chilies and garlic.
Pound the chilies, garlic and toasted shrimp paste in a mortar until coarse, or pulse in a small food processor.
Stir in the lime juice, [[1 tsp]] sugar and [[0.5 tsp]] salt.
Taste and adjust with more lime or salt. Serve fresh with rice, fried fish or grilled meats.
Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment.
Beat [[0.5 cup]] softened ghee with [[0.5 cup]] powdered sugar for 3 minutes until pale and creamy.
Stir in [[0.5 tsp]] vanilla and a pinch of salt.
Sift in [[1.5 cups]] flour and [[0.25 cup]] milk powder and fold gently into a soft dough.
Chill the dough for 15 minutes so it is easy to shape.
Roll into small balls about 1 inch wide and set them 1 inch apart on the sheet. Flatten each lightly with a fork.
Bake 18 to 20 minutes until pale gold on the bottom edges.
Cool on the sheet for 10 minutes, since the cookies are very fragile when hot, then move to a rack.
